I'll read the project so the update matches what you actually shipped, then write it as a short hackathon update in your voice.

Say it like this. Drop your real credit number in the blank.

Hey, quick update. Friction Fixer v1 is out and running. You point it at a site, start a run, and the agents do the rest. The analyst looks at the numbers and picks one change. The builder edits the code and opens a pull request. The reviewer checks whether bounce rate actually dropped. If it did, the change stays. If it didn't, the agent undoes it and the next run tries something else.

The agents are working fine. Every run is in neatlogs, step by step, so you can see what they did. Entire is on the repo too, so the reasoning behind each code change is saved as checkpoints.

I'll match the pitch to what the product actually does, then write the intro in your voice.

Say it like this.

I'm building Friction Fixer, a platform that runs agents that fix your website by themselves. You don't hand it a list of bugs. You connect your analytics, like PostHog or Mixpanel, it reads how people actually use the site, and it writes a plan from that. Then it opens a pull request on the GitHub repo you dropped in, ships the change, and keeps checking whether it helped. If it didn't, it undoes it and tries again. You drop the repo, and the site gets better without you doing the work.

I'll drop the link so you can try it.

v1 is out. The agents run. Sometimes a run fails and I'm fixing that, but yeah, super excited to see how this goes. Every run is in neatlogs if you want to watch what they did, and Entire has the checkpoints for why each code change was made.

One thing to know before you record: v1 still runs on mock visitor numbers. PostHog and Mixpanel are on the onboarding screen, but live analytics is not wired up yet. If someone opens the project, "it reads your actual PostHog data" will not match what is running.
